title: wartime oil diet boosts renewables 2026 09 04
text:
Sept 4 (Reuters) - Greetings People of Switch: Ross Kerber here writing a weekly version of this newsletter, standing in for Sharon Kimathi who is away until the week of September 14.
Economics 101 says if you want people to use less of something, raise its price. That's what's happened as a result of the shipping constraints caused by the Iran war, with various stories and studies showing how consumer fuel demand has dropped dramatically so far ​this year.
You can read more about the trends in this week's main story, below, plus my own pet theory about why Washington may not be so concerned about oil price hikes.
I've also ‌got links to our coverage of the role climate change might play in deadly floods; a rethink of the resilience of robusta coffee; and a look at the El Nino weather phenomenon.

* Oil crunch fuels green shift
Countries around the world are learning to use less fuel since the U.S.-Iran war sharply cut supplies and sent pump prices soaring.
My colleagues have covered this trend plenty on our newswire with individual stories, so it seems like a good time to round up the articles to ​get at the bigger picture.
The starting place is China, the world's largest emitter of carbon dioxide. Carbon emissions fell 1% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, according to a recent Centre for Research on ​Energy and Clean Air analysis.
The decrease was driven by a 9% fall in oil consumption as consumers moved to electric vehicles faster than anticipated, a trend unlikely to be reversed.
China's ⁠experience is just a snapshot of a broader trend in which governments are accelerating a renewables build-out to cut dependence on fossil fuel imports.
Global renewable power output is soaring, and the International Energy Agency (IEA) expects it to become ​the top electricity source for the first time this year.
In 2027, the IEA expects coal output to dip by 0.7%, but gas-fired power generation to rise 1.5% from this year's levels. Curbing climate change will require even more renewable energy ​and investments in power grids and energy storage, my colleagues reported.
Speaking of economic adjustments, the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas has an interesting set of working papers on the war's impact on energy prices and the economy.
One of the most interesting dates from June, titled "How Times Have Changed
, opens new tab
: The Impact of the 2026 Iran War on the U.S. Economy." The perhaps-intuitive finding is that as a net oil exporter, the U.S. is much less exposed to disruption than it was in the 1970s.
This also got me thinking: how come higher ​energy prices haven't prompted equally big moves away from fossil fuels in the U.S.? One answer may be in another finding of the paper, that the U.S. is better positioned to weather the supply disruption than most other ​countries. As the authors state:
"Our model implies that the 15% global oil supply disruption causes a much larger decline in real GDP growth in the rest of the world than in the U.S. Whereas annualized real GDP growth declines by 1.73 percentage ‌points in the ⁠rest of the world, it declines by only 0.26 percentage points in the U.S. This result stands in sharp contrast to 1980, when the impact on growth was quite similar across the two country blocs, with both contracting by about 1.8 percentage points. This asymmetry reflects the structural transformation of the U.S. oil sector, which has insulated the U.S. from foreign oil supply disruptions."
The observation would give U.S. President Donald Trump space to continue to put military pressure on Iran while waiting for sanctions and pressure from other countries to sway Iran's rulers into a favorable settlement. But I bet more than pure economic theory will be needed to end this war.
* Talking Points
- Pity the corn: Record heatwaves and chronic water ​shortages are shrinking maize harvests for farmers across central ​and eastern Europe, reshaping a region long seen as a ⁠pillar of European grain production.
- Climate and rock: By destabilizing high-mountain rock and ice, climate change could bring on more disasters like the catastrophic August 26 flood along the border between Nepal and China's Tibet, scientists say. You can watch our newscast on the matter here.
- Coffee myth: Robusta coffee may not be as climate-resilient as thought, a new paper found, triggering a rethink ​of the industry's answer to climate change. As our story states, "the new paper in Sustainable Development found that previous assessments should be considered provisional at best. It cited ​research errors such as treating irrigated ⁠farms as optimal growing areas." Drink up!
- Fishery powers: A council created by Congress to help the U.S. commerce secretary manage the nation's fisheries exercised unconstitutional powers, a federal appeals court said. But it declined to strike down a rule limiting the catch of a Gulf of Mexico gag grouper.
* ESG Lens
Look out for what become the strongest-ever El Niño weather phenomenon, the World Meteorological Organization said, raising risks of extreme weather into 2027.
The U.N. weather agency forecast a near 100% likelihood that El Niño would persist ⁠through February, fuelled ​by exceptionally warm Pacific Ocean temperatures.
El Niño is a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific caused by weakening trade ​winds. A very strong El Niño can fuel extreme weather, such as droughts and typhoons.
While it is a naturally occurring phenomenon and not directly linked to fossil fuel-driven climate change, it can be intensified by warmer ocean temperatures.
